phonemes.desc: A short open a followed by the privative prefix — a-, 'without' — the negation that is the whole name.
The palatalized nasal ṅ before g — saṅga, 'clinging, attachment,' from √sañj.
A light final syllable — Asanga, 'without attachment,' a name that is already a doctrine.

pronunciation.approximation: 'UH-sung-guh' — short vowels, even stress; the ṅg is the nasal 'ng' of 'singer,' not 'finger.'

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: a- (privative) + saṅga 'clinging, attachment,' from √sañj — 'without attachment' (Monier-Williams); a name that doubles as the aim of his school

kin.label: Pāli
kin.form: Asaṅga — the same compound, attested across the canon as an ideal adjective long before it was a man's name

kin.label: Tibetan
kin.form: Thogs med — 'unobstructed,' the standard translation; his half-brother Vasubandhu is dByig gnyen, 'Treasure of Gems'

pronunciation.note: Tier 2: 'Asanga' is ASCII-canonical in spelling; the restoration restores the name's meaning — a- + saṅga, 'without attachment' — which is also the psychological thesis of the Yogācāra school he founded.

domains.title: Asanga
domains.subtitle: Without Attachment — Founder of Yogācāra, the Practice of Mind Only
domains.lead: Asanga (c. 4th–5th century CE) is the founder of Yogācāra, the Buddhist school that analyzed consciousness itself — the ālayavijñāna store-mind, the three natures, the construction of the world by perception — and the man who, by tradition, received the future Buddha Maitreya's five treatises on a visit to Tuṣita heaven.

cards.name: Yogācāra
cards.desc: The 'practice of yoga' school — Abhidharma rewritten as psychology: suffering located in the structure of consciousness itself.

cards.name: The Vision of Maitreya
cards.desc: Twelve years of retreat, a dying dog, and transport to Tuṣita heaven — where the future Buddha dictated the five great treatises.

cards.name: The Two Brothers
cards.desc: He and his half-brother Vasubandhu wrote half the Indian Mahāyāna — the gentle ambush that converted the greatest critic of the Mahāyāna.

cards.name: Mind-Only
cards.desc: The world as construction of consciousness — 'mind-only,' his opponents' nickname, became the school's thesis and modern cognitive science's ancestor.

symbols.name: The wounded dog
symbols.meaning: The dying dog whose maggots he moved with his tongue — the act of compassion that revealed Maitreya, and the founding parable of Yogācāra: insight comes through the heart, not the head

symbols.name: Maitreya's tower
symbols.meaning: Tuṣita heaven, where the five treatises were received — Yogācāra's scriptural charter is literally from the future

symbols.name: The mirror
symbols.meaning: The school's favorite image in later East Asian art — perception like a mirror: images arise, none stick; Asanga's name, 'without attachment,' is the mirror wiped clean

symbols.name: The storehouse (ālaya)
symbols.meaning: The ālayavijñāna, the warehouse consciousness where seeds of karma sleep and sprout — his school's most influential and most argued concept

symbols.name: The three natures
symbols.meaning: Imagined, dependent, perfected — Asanga's map of how the mind builds its world and how it sees through the building

mythology.lead: Asanga's mythology is the hagiography of a psychologist: the vision that founded his school came through compassion for a dog, and his school's charter texts were, by tradition, dictated by the future Buddha — scholarship's verdict is that Asanga wrote them himself, which changes nothing about the parable.

myths.title: Two Brothers, One Teaching
myths.text: Asanga and his younger half-brother Vasubandhu — arguably the two most consequential Buddhist philosophers after Nāgārjuna — were born, the story runs (Xuanzang preserves it in his Great Tang Records of the Western Regions), to a brahmin of Kauśika lineage; their mother, the legend adds, resolved that one son should master the Mahāyāna and the other its rival, the analytical Abhidharma of Kaśmīr. Vasubandhu became the encyclopedist of the Abhidharmakośa; Asanga wandered and meditated until he founded Yogācāra. Then the elder brother executed the gentlest ambush in the history of ideas: feigning a mortal illness, he had disciples read him a Mahāyāna sūtra and plant objections that only the Mahāyāna could answer — until the great critic recanted on the spot and joined the school he had spent his career refuting. Vasubandhu's conversion doubled the school's firepower: the Viṃśikā and Trimśikā became its core. The myth explains a real fact: half of the Indian Mahāyāna was written by one family — brotherly love as the engine of a philosophical revolution.

myths.title: Twelve Years, a Wounded Dog, and Maitreya
myths.text: The founding vision of Yogācāra is a story about compassion first. Asanga, the tradition says (Xuanzang; the Tibetan historians Bu ston and Tāranātha repeat it), spent twelve years in solitary retreat awaiting a vision of the future Buddha Maitreya — and saw nothing. Despairing on his way down the mountain, he met a dog dying in the road, its open wounds alive with maggots; to save both creature and worms he cut flesh from his own thigh and reached to lift the maggots with his tongue. The dog vanished: it was Maitreya. The bodhisattva then carried Asanga bodily to Tuṣita heaven, where he received the five great treatises — Abhisamayālaṃkāra, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, Madhyāntavibhāga, Dharmadharmatāvibhāga, Ratnagotravibhāga. Modern scholarship — Frauwallner most forcefully — argues Asanga wrote them himself. The interpretive point survives either way: a philosophy of mind founded by a man whose breakthrough came through the gut — the dying dog was the last rung of the ladder.

myths.title: Yogācāra, the Practice of Mind-Only
myths.text: What Asanga built — with Vasubandhu and their lineage — the tradition called Yogācāra, "practice of yoga," and its opponents called cittamātra, "mind-only." Its masterworks, the Mahāyāna-saṃgraha ("Compendium of the Mahāyāna") and the Abhidharmasamuccaya, set out a psychology of awakening: the store-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), a deep repository in which the seeds of deeds and habits sleep, waiting to sprout as the world; the three natures — the imagined (the snake), the dependent (the rope), the perfected (the seeing); and the radical claim that the "external world" is a construction of consciousness, no more independent than a dream is independent of the dreamer. The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra supplied the school's scriptural charter, with its doctrine of the three turnings of the wheel. The interpretive meaning: suffering was re-described from metaphysics into psychology — and liberation as a rewiring of perception, perception seen at last as the whole stage.

myths.title: From Nālandā to the Faxiang School
myths.text: Yogācāra conquered China by land and sea. Paramārtha carried its first full synthesis in the 6th century; then Xuanzang, after his epochal pilgrimage of 629–645, studied it at Nālandā under Śīlabhadra — Asanga's doctrinal great-grandson across five generations of masters — and brought back hundreds of manuscripts by pack animal. His synthesis, the Cheng weishi lun ("Discourse on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only," completed 659), founded the Chinese Faxiang school; carried to Japan it became Hossō, the school of Kōfukuji, and its Kegon cousin built the great Huayan systems on Yogācāra bones. The line then looped home: Tibetan translators rendered Asanga and Vasubandhu entire, and every Tibetan debate courtyard still argues their three-nature scheme. The interpretive lesson: a school born in a retreat hut on the Ganges plain became the common grammar of the Asian philosophy of mind — the one Buddhist system a modern cognitive scientist can read with almost no translation.

lore.syncretism: Yogācāra's fate was absorption: too useful to defeat, it was eaten by its rivals. In India, the great synthesis of the 8th century married Asanga's psychology to Nāgārjuna's emptiness — Śāntarakṣita's Madhyāmakālaṃkāra declared the two schools two doors into one house, a verdict all later Indian Buddhism accepted. In East Asia, Yogācāra merged with Huayan's cosmos and Tiantai's Lotus hermeneutics, surviving explicitly only in Japan's Hossō school while secretly structuring everything else. In Tibet, Asanga is 'the two brothers' half of every curriculum — the Abhisamayālaṃkāra is the master commentary on the Prajñāpāramitā that Nāgārjuna supposedly rescued from the sea. The modern meeting is stranger: William James and the Yogācārins now read each other — 'pure experience' and 'mind-only' are neighbors across a century, and the ālayavijñāna reappears in cognitive science as 'predictive processing.' The school named 'practice' became, in the end, the theory everyone practices against.
lore.culturalLegacy: Asanga's legacy is institutional and conceptual at once. Nālandā, where his lineage taught for seven centuries, is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the name of India's modern flagship university; the Tibetan monastic curriculum still opens philosophy with his Abhisamayālaṃkāra, memorized line by line across every shedra from Lhasa to Mundgod. In East Asia the Faxiang/Hossō line, though small, preserved his texts when India lost them — Xuanzang's rescue of the manuscripts is itself one of the great stories of civilization's luggage. And the concepts migrated far beyond Buddhism: the store-consciousness anticipates the unconscious, the three natures prefigure constructivist accounts of perception, and 'mind-only' is quoted in contemporary philosophy of mind and machine-learning debates alike. A man whose name means 'without attachment' ended up attached to everything.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Asanga's school asks the question most traditions bury: not 'what is the world?' but 'who is building it right now?' His answer — the mind, constructing its world and mistaking the construction for the thing — was psychology three centuries before Augustine and fifteen before the laboratory. But his founding parable keeps the science honest: the vision came not from analysis but from a dying dog, and the first act of the school's founder was to bleed for a stranger's wounds.

There is a lesson in the pairing. Yogācāra's map of mind — seeds, stores, three natures — is as intricate as any in antiquity, yet the tradition insists it was dictated by compassion itself, in the form of Maitreya. Analysis without tenderness, Asanga's life says, is just another attachment — to being right. The name is the teaching: without attachment, even to the map. A psychologist who knew that the last obstacle is the theory of the obstacle.

lore.archaeology: Asanga left no monument of his own, and his century left few datable ones — the 4th–5th-century Buddhist world of northern India is known mostly through the pilgrim accounts (Faxian, then Xuanzang) and the great monastic cities they describe. Nālandā, excavated by the Archaeological Survey of India from 1915 and now a UNESCO site, preserves the excavated grid of his school's eventual home: eleven monasteries and six temples in brick, the sarai and the stūpas. The Ajanta caves' later viharas (5th–6th c.) show the scholastic monasticism his movement filled — rows of cells, lecture halls, painted jātakas. His true artifacts are textual: the five Maitreya treatises survive in hundreds of Sanskrit fragments and complete Tibetan and Chinese translations, their colophons still arguing about who wrote them — which is, for a school about the construction of authorship, exactly right.
